case_study_insert.main_stem: Ferndale Green Steel (FGS) is a public limited company in the steel recycling sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2016 by Raya Ferndale, the business melts scrap steel in electric arc furnaces to produce certified low-carbon steel for construction and manufacturing and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. FGS plans to invest $2,400,000 in a new automated scrap-sorting line and baghouse filter, financed by a $1,300,000 share issue and $1,100,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $3,600,000 a year, a variable cost of $440 a unit and a selling price of $620, and currently produces 34,000 units a year. FGS faces two operational problems: absenteeism has reached 10% and scrap contamination is driving rework in the melt shop.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Report — Q3 2025: The melt shop processed 8,600 tonnes of scrap steel at a rework rate of 2.2%, down from 3.4% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 12 to 7 per month. Market research of 250 industrial buyers found that 74% would pay up to 8% more for certified low-carbon steel. Average delivery lead time is 6 days, and scrap-sorting trials have lifted metal recovery to 92%. A training needs analysis shows 22 of 120 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new shredder; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ferndale Green Steel for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, a 0.75 percentage point rise, lifting borrowing costs on the variable portion of long-term loans. (2) The national living wage will rise by 6.6% from $12.30 to $13.11 per hour from April 2026, raising wage costs across the melt shop. (3) Steel scrap costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year and industrial electricity costs 9.5%, while producer price inflation is running at 4.6% and construction steel demand grew 3.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: FGS plans to finance part of its $2,400,000 expansion with a share issue. Explain two advantages for FGS of using a share issue instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises finance without creating interest or repayment obligations, protecting FGS's cash flow at a time when the company already carries fixed costs of $3,600,000 a year and services $240,000–$310,000 of annual interest. Avoiding extra debt repayments on the $2,400,000 automated scrap-sorting line leaves more operating cash to absorb the 11.2% rise in scrap costs and the 9.5% rise in industrial electricity prices — critical for a furnaces business whose variable cost is already $440 a unit.

Point 2: New equity strengthens FGS's balance sheet and credit rating, making later borrowing cheaper if the line outperforms. There is also no collateral at risk: if low-carbon steel demand disappoints, shareholders bear the loss rather than the melt shop being repossessed. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders' control and future dividends, but Raya Ferndale judged this worthwhile to fund the certified low-carbon programme that 74% of 250 surveyed industrial buyers would pay 8% more for.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Ferndale Green Steel and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: FGS is launching its certified low-carbon steel for construction buyers. Consider advertising in national business newspapers, a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers, or sponsorship of the Green Manufacturing Expo. Which should FGS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National business newspaper advertising: Full-page adverts in national papers would reach a broad business audience and raise FGS's profile among institutional investors as well as buyers, signalling the permanence of a public limited company. However, national print is very expensive, much of the readership is irrelevant to steel specification, response is hard to measure, and a single issue barely dents the procurement habits of the 74% of buyers willing to pay 8% more for certified low-carbon steel.

Sponsorship of the Green Manufacturing Expo: Exhibiting and speaking at a green-manufacturing expo would put FGS face-to-face with sustainability officers, specifiers and major contractors, with strong credibility from the 92% scrap recovery and certified low-carbon positioning. The weaknesses are high one-off fees, attendance limited to event days, and poor reach for the hundreds of regional fabricators and distributors who also buy steel; it builds depth, not breadth.

A targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers: Precise targeting by industry, role and company size lets FGS deliver technical carbon-footprint content directly to the people who specify steel — at low cost per reached decision-maker, with measurable enquiries, and sustained all year. It suits a B2B technical product perfectly, though it requires continuous quality content and may under-reach less digitally active small buyers.

Recommendation: FGS should choose the targeted LinkedIn campaign. It reaches the precise procurement audience identified in research, costs least per qualified lead, runs year-round beyond one expo, and produces the measurable enquiry data a public limited company needs to justify the $2,400,000 investment to shareholders. Business-newspaper advertising is rejected as too expensive and too broad; the expo is rejected as too narrow and event-limited, though FGS could add a small stand later once the certified range wins its first major framing contract.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of FGS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FGS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why business newspapers and the expo are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for FGS of using team working in the melt shop to tackle its 10% absenteeism and scrap contamination.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working pools the furnace crew's practical knowledge of why scrap contamination happens, generating joint fixes such as better pre-sort checks and clearer signals between cranes and furnace operators. Teams also cover for each other during absences, keeping the melt shop running at 8,600 tonnes a quarter instead of losing output when one of the 120 staff is off — directly relieving the 10% absenteeism and the rework driven by contaminated charges.

Point 2: Teams build peer accountability and social support, satisfying Maslow's social needs and reversing the isolation behind high absence. Operators who help each other also learn faster on the new shredder, support the 22 staff awaiting training, and sustain the improvement from a 3.4% to 2.2% rework rate. Lower absenteeism and rework cut overtime, scrap-disposal and quality-failure costs, protecting the $620 selling price and the margins FGS needs to justify the $2,400,000 expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FGS's absenteeism, rework and expansion.

questions.question_text: FGS must upskill 22 scrap-sorting operators for the new automated line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college at $1,100 per employee. Which should FGS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside the shredder and furnace is directly relevant to FGS's own scrap grades, recovery targets and safety regime, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 22 operators productive — protecting throughput of 8,600 tonnes a quarter and the drop in rework from 3.4% to 2.2%. Weaknesses: trainers are production staff whose own duties suffer, informal bad habits spread, and no external certificate is issued to demonstrate competence to clients auditing FGS's certified low-carbon claims.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $1,100 per employee would cost $24,200 for all 22 — easily affordable against a $2,400,000 investment. It provides structured, up-to-date theory (metallurgy, sorting standards, safety regulation) and recognised certification, strengthening FGS's certified credentials with buyers willing to pay 8% more. However, it removes over 18% of the workforce from the melt shop for course days, risks delivery delays, and the generic syllabus may not match FGS's exact shredder settings, so site coaching would still be required.

Decision: FGS should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, reserving college certification for two lead operators and the quality supervisor. This is the cheapest and most machine-specific route, keeps the furnaces fed, and avoids withdrawing 22 of 120 staff while absenteeism is already 10%. Full off-the-job training is rejected as too disruptive to the delivery schedule and poor value for operators who need hands-on sorting practice; the $24,200 would be better spent on a follow-up QA audit once the line is stable and rework falls toward 1.5%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to FGS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of FGS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of FGS with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FGS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $3,600,000 ÷ ($620 − $440) = $3,600,000 ÷ $180 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $620 − $440 = $180. Answer: contribution per unit is $180.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FGS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. FGS's managers can compare the 20,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 34,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 14,000 units, and use this headroom to judge whether to accelerate the new sorting line towards full utilisation.
2. Contribution per unit of $180 lets managers model the effect of a 5% premium price increase for certified low-carbon steel, which would lift contribution to $211, and judge how much volume FGS could lose before total contribution falls.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $3,600,000 and contribution per unit helps managers test whether the $2,400,000 expansion pays back via incremental units, and set the volume targets needed to justify the share issue and retained-profit mix.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($3,600,000 ÷ 34,000 units + $440 = $545.88 a unit) to benchmark each quarter, pinpoint the contamination driving the 2.2% rework rate, and decide whether to renegotiate scrap supply contracts amid the 11.2% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $180 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 14,000 units against 34,000-unit output; premium-pricing modelling for the certified range against $3,600,000 fixed costs; expansion affordability testing for the $2,400,000 investment; and unit-cost benchmarking at $545.88 to tackle 2.2% rework and scrap contamination.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FGS's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has FGS's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 37.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 23.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $15,800,000 revenue − $10,270,000 cost of sales = $5,530,000; 2025 gross profit = $18,400,000 − $11,500,000 = $6,900,000. 2024 operating profit of $1,580,000 ÷ revenue of $15,800,000 = 10.0%; 2025 operating profit of $2,208,000 ÷ revenue of $18,400,000 = 12.0%. 2024 operating profit of $1,580,000 ÷ capital employed of $7,900,000 = 20.0%; 2025 operating profit of $2,208,000 ÷ capital employed of $9,600,000 = 23.0%. Revenue rose $2,600,000 while cost of sales grew just $1,230,000, so gross profit rose $1,370,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has improved on every measure. The shift toward certified low-carbon steel lifted the gross margin by 2.5 percentage points to 37.5%, and operating profit grew faster than revenue — up nearly 40% to $2,208,000 — showing genuine operating leverage from higher throughput and lower rework, not just price inflation. Capital employed grew $1,700,000 for the sorting line and baghouse, yet returns on that capital rose from 20.0% to 23.0%, comfortably covering the $310,000 interest payable. Risks persist: scrap and electricity inflation (11.2% and 9.5%) could squeeze the gross margin if contract prices lag, and 10% absenteeism adds overtime costs that trim operating profit.

Conclusion: FGS's profitability has improved. Margins and returns on capital both strengthened in 2025, and the gains are structural — better recovery of 92%, certified premium pricing and falling rework — rather than one-off. To keep improving, FGS must lock in scrap contracts, fix absenteeism and ensure the new line delivers the volume needed to dilute the higher capital base.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether FGS's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FGS of producing certified low-carbon steel from recycled scrap instead of from virgin ore.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified low-carbon steel from recycled scrap matches the 74% of 250 surveyed industrial buyers willing to pay up to 8% more, letting FGS charge a premium that protects its $180 contribution per unit even as scrap costs rise 11.2%. It also uses roughly a quarter of the energy of primary steelmaking, supports FGS's environmental brand with construction specifiers, and — reinforced by the 92% scrap recovery rate — builds the certified credentials that differentiate FGS from conventional mills competing for the $620-a-unit market.

Disadvantage: Recycled scrap quality is inconsistent — copper and tin contamination force costly sorting and rework (the very problem the $2,400,000 automated line must fix) and can cap the grades FGS can certify. Scrap price volatility (up 11.2% year-on-year) also destabilises the $440 variable cost; if FGS cannot pass rises on, contribution shrinks and the returns needed to justify the share issue and retained-profit mix are at risk, while contamination-driven rework at 2.2% still erodes margins.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FGS's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.6% living wage increase and the 11.2% rise in steel scrap costs will affect FGS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): On the variable portion of FGS's borrowings, a 0.75 percentage point rise on around $310,000 of annual interest adds roughly $44,000 a year — noticeable but absorbable, and largely avoidable once loans are refinanced or fixed. Higher rates may also lift shareholders' required returns, but the direct cash impact is the smallest of the three for FGS.

Living wage increase (6.6%, to $13.11 per hour): FGS employs 120 staff, mostly in the melt shop on hourly rates near or above the living wage. The rise adds about $0.81 an hour, or roughly $1,685 per worker a year — around $200,000 across the whole workforce if applied broadly. That is over 9% of 2025 operating profit and will press on the democratic leaders recently to hold pay settlements without productivity gains through team working and lower rework.

Scrap cost inflation (11.2% year-on-year, plus 9.5% electricity): Scrap likely represents 60–70% of the $440 variable cost (about $270–$300). An 11.2% rise adds roughly $30–$34 per unit; at 34,000 units that is $1,020,000–$1,156,000 a year — potentially wiping out half of operating profit before price recovery. Electricity adds hundreds of thousands more. Recovery depends on passing costs into contract steel prices, where FGS has the 8% certified premium as partial cover.

Conclusion: The 11.2% scrap cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 34,000 units sold and is an order of magnitude larger than the wage bill increase or the interest rise, directly compressing the $180 contribution and the certified premium FGS relies on. FGS must lock in multi-year scrap contracts, accelerate sorting-line throughput and push through indexed pricing; the wage rise is the second-largest threat and the rate rise the least damaging, though all three demand margin discipline through 2027.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FGS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FGS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FGS with a well-justified judgement that scrap-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
